title: "Where New Evidence Matters"
description: "Which new evidence would most improve urban climate decisions?"
canonical-url: "/research/where-new-evidence-matters.html"

<!-- Generated by scripts/generate_site.py; do not edit. -->

Once the limits of existing evidence become visible, a further problem arises: deciding what evidence should be produced next. Urban climate research often treats an unstudied place, population or intervention as a research gap. Yet absence alone does not establish value. Some gaps may have little bearing on current decisions, while a strategically chosen case, causal evaluation, comparison or dataset may resolve uncertainty for many cities.

Where New Evidence Matters examines which additional knowledge could alter an appraisal, distinguish between competing explanations, clarify a mechanism, correct a consequential exclusion or expand the range of cities able to learn. It connects evidence mapping with research design and decision analysis, asking not simply where knowledge is missing, but where producing it could change what cities understand or do. The theme does not seek a universal ranking of research priorities; the value of new evidence depends on the decision, uncertainty and community it is intended to serve.

::: {.what-this-changes}
**The proposition.** The size of an evidence gap and the value of filling it are different questions.
:::

**What this theme does not assume.** A data gap, new tool or under-studied location is not automatically a research priority. New evidence matters where its production could materially change understanding, appraisal or action.

These are possible directions for future research, not active or funded projects.

<span class="sr-only">Each card retains the full status: Research idea · not currently an active or funded project</span>

This layout provides a reading hierarchy; it is not a ranking of research priority, funding readiness or importance.

Research resources could generate more cumulative knowledge if case selection considered how much a new case might change inference for other cities.</p><h4>How we might study it</h4><p>Hierarchical models and value-of-information analysis, combined with active-learning approaches, could identify cases whose evidence would most change current estimates or classifications.</p><p class="idea-qualification"><strong>Analytical boundary.</strong> This is an academic research question, not a proposal for a single public city-ranking or marginal-learning-value score.</p><ul class="method-list"><li>hierarchical modelling</li><li>value-of-information analysis</li><li>active learning</li></ul><p class="idea-reader"><strong>Reader or decision at stake:</strong> Comparative researchers selecting cases.</p></article><article class="idea-card signature-idea" data-narrative-tier="signature"><p class="idea-badge">Research idea</p><p class="sr-only">Research idea · not currently an active or funded project</p><h3>When is there enough evidence?</h3><p class="idea-question">At what point does another case study add little to understanding, and when should research effort shift to a different mechanism, population or place?</p><h4>Why this question matters</h4><p>Research fields may continue accumulating similar cases because data are accessible, even after the marginal contribution to understanding has declined. Without defensible stopping rules, research may reproduce well-covered questions while more consequential uncertainties remain unresolved.</p><h4>How we might study it</h4><p>Sequential meta-analysis and explicit stopping rules could estimate diminishing informational returns, while sensitivity analysis could test whether apparent saturation hides neglected contexts.</p><ul class="method-list"><li>sequential meta-analysis</li><li>stopping-rule analysis</li><li>evidence-saturation analysis</li></ul><p class="idea-reader"><strong>Reader or decision at stake:</strong> Research funders and evidence-synthesis teams.</p></article></div><h3 class="idea-group-heading">Additional directions</h3><div class="idea-grid"><article class="idea-card" data-narrative-tier="additional"><p class="idea-badge">Research idea</p><p class="sr-only">Research idea · not currently an active or funded project</p><h3>When evaluation could change the decision</h3><p class="idea-question">Which urban climate policies sit close enough to an adoption, design or investment threshold that stronger causal evidence could change the decision?</p><h4>Why this question matters</h4><p>Evaluation resources are often directed toward visible programmes rather than decisions where uncertainty is actually pivotal. A rigorous evaluation has greater practical value when its result could alter a live choice, rather than merely produce a better estimate after the decision is effectively settled.</p><h4>How we might study it</h4><p>Decision-pathway mapping and threshold analysis could identify consequential uncertainties, followed by an assessment of where natural experiments, matched comparisons or synthetic controls are feasible.</p><ul class="method-list"><li>decision-pathway mapping</li><li>threshold analysis</li><li>natural experiments</li></ul><p class="idea-reader"><strong>Reader or decision at stake:</strong> Researchers designing causal evaluations around live decisions.</p></article><article class="idea-card" data-narrative-tier="additional"><p class="idea-badge">Research idea</p><p class="sr-only">Research idea · not currently an active or funded project</p><h3>Which disagreement deserves replication?</h3><p class="idea-question">When urban climate studies reach conflicting conclusions, which disagreements reflect context, method or chance, and which are worth resolving?</p><h4>Why this question matters</h4><p>Calls for replication often treat all findings similarly even though some disagreements concern inconsequential details and others destabilise widely used assumptions. Strategically targeted replication could clarify whether disagreement reflects genuine contextual heterogeneity or avoidable methodological differences.</p><h4>How we might study it</h4><p>Structured replication portfolios, multiverse analysis and Bayesian model comparison could distinguish methodological disagreement from genuine contextual variation.</p><ul class="method-list"><li>coordinated replication</li><li>multiverse analysis</li><li>Bayesian model comparison</li></ul><p class="idea-reader"><strong>Reader or decision at stake:</strong> Evidence-synthesis teams selecting replication questions.</p></article><article class="idea-card" data-narrative-tier="additional"><p class="idea-badge">Research idea</p><p class="sr-only">Research idea · not currently an active or funded project</p><h3>Which exclusions change the answer?</h3><p class="idea-question">Which absent places or populations would materially alter an appraisal, causal estimate or claim about generalisability if they were represented?</p><h4>Why this question matters</h4><p>Evidence maps can identify exclusions, but the number of missing places or populations does not show whether their inclusion would change the answer. Prioritising consequential exclusions could connect representational justice with the analytical effect of missing evidence.</p><h4>How we might study it</h4><p>Evidence-gap mapping could be combined with population, vulnerability and policy data, followed by counterfactual reweighting and participatory priority setting.</p><ul class="method-list"><li>evidence-gap mapping</li><li>counterfactual reweighting</li><li>participatory priority setting</li></ul><p class="idea-reader"><strong>Reader or decision at stake:</strong> Research funders and communities defining consequential exclusions.</p></article><article class="idea-card" data-narrative-tier="additional"><p class="idea-badge">Research idea</p><p class="sr-only">Research idea · not currently an active or funded project</p><h3>A coordinated network of urban evaluations</h3><p class="idea-question">Could cities design complementary evaluations that answer a shared question rather than producing isolated case studies?</p><h4>Why this question matters</h4><p>Individually useful studies may remain collectively incomparable because they measure different outcomes, use incompatible designs or repeat the same evidentiary limitations. Coordinated evaluation could produce stronger cumulative evidence while retaining local adaptation and institutional relevance.</p><h4>How we might study it</h4><p>An adaptive multi-city design could combine common outcome measures, staggered implementation, federated data and pre-agreed comparative hypotheses while allowing local variation.</p><ul class="method-list"><li>adaptive multi-site evaluation</li><li>federated analysis</li><li>staggered implementation</li></ul><p class="idea-reader"><strong>Reader or decision at stake:</strong> Researchers and city networks designing complementary evaluations.</p></article></div>

## How this connects

- **Input from [Geographies of Climate Learning](/research/geographies-of-climate-learning.html):** Mapping the reach and limits of existing knowledge reveals which unresolved questions could be consequential enough to justify new research.
- **Next stage — [Modes of Climate Delivery](/research/modes-of-climate-delivery.html):** New evidence matters most when it changes what decision-makers understand about how climate action can be delivered or what it may cause.
- **Return loop:** Consequences generate new evidence, reveal unresolved questions and revise what other cities may plausibly learn.
